*.why: A command a tool prints for the reader to run next is spelled as the nv subcommand that replaces the Python tool, which keeps the Python tool's name.

brief.why: A message names the program that printed it.

peek.pattern: ^-- (that is \d+ calls in a row|you have now fetched) .*\n
peek.why: The footer's advice reads a per-session ledger both programs write, and a parity case runs them at once, so which one counted first is a race.

splice.why: A message names the program that printed it.

splice.pattern: -- see this script's docstring for the patch format$
splice.replace: -- `bun nv splice --help` prints the patch format
splice.why: nv has no docstring to point at, so the hint names the command that prints the format.
Python and Bun each word an operating system error their own way, and both name the file.
nv writes a CRLF target back with CRLF, and splice.py writes it back with LF. Keeping a file's line endings is what both claim to do, and only nv does it.

splice.pattern: ^AGENTS\.md forbids carrying file content through a shell[\s\S]*?never from the command line\.\n\n
splice.why: nv's help starts at the invocation forms. Why the blocks come from a file is in the command's module comment, where a person changing it reads it.

splice.pattern:
which is the older one-file form and still
works\. (\*\*Either way the whole) (patch applies or none of it does\*\* -- every block in every file is)
matched (before a single byte is) (written, so a stale anchor in the last file cannot leave the first)
one half-edited\.
splice.replace:
which is the one-file form. $1
$2 matched $3
$4 one half-edited.
splice.why: nv's help does not call the one-file form older, since nv has only ever had it, and the paragraph wraps where the shorter sentence leaves it.

layout.why: A message names the program that printed it.

directives.why: A message names the program that printed it.

reference.why: A message names the program that printed it.

disk.why: A message names the program that printed it.

migration.why: Python prints the inventory's path with the platform's separator. nv prints every path with forward slashes.

owners.why: A message names the program that printed it.
Python names a gap by its line and its number in the module doc, which are positions. nv names it by its record's slug, which never moves.
The other half of the rewrite above: the slug is erased so the module and the title are what is compared.
An item that opens on no bold run is led by its whole text in Python, cut at 78 characters. Its record's title is the first sentence, so a gap line is compared up to its first sentence's end.
nv reads the gap records, not the module docs they were imported from.

owners.pattern: a numbered item under a `# Known gaps` block, tagged with its owner
owners.replace: a gap record, naming the goal or milestone that owns it
owners.why: The same register, described as the record nv reads.
nv reads the playbook bullet records, not the fragments they were imported from.
A bullet record's `until` is a field, not a trailer.
A block is a module doc's grouping, and a gap record has none.

A gap object is a record in nv (slug, module, title, text) and a parsed doc item in Python (file, line, block, item). The counts per owner under `registers` are what callers read, and they are compared.

decisions.why: A message names the program that printed it.
Python prints the rendered paths with the platform's separator. nv prints every path with forward slashes.
The rendered page names the command that renders it, and nv renders the same bytes as the Python tool until the cutover. The `*` entry rewrites the Python side's copy of that line.
`--work` quotes each record's In short text as it is written, and a record names Python tools. The `*` entry rewrites the Python side's copy of those lines, so nv's copy gets the same rewrite.

rules.why: A message names the program that printed it.

records.why: A **Depends on:** field that is only links is stored as its record numbers, so the period the prose closes the list with is not kept, and `--graph` prints the links alone.

proofs.why: A message names the program that printed it, and the word dossier leaves the tree.
The command a line tells the reader to run is `nv proofs`, which replaces `dossier.py` under a new name.
`dossier.py`'s `php_twins` reads the spec's signature cell where it means the Replaces cell, so it never finds a twin. `nv proofs` reads the Replaces cell.

chain.replace: chain: every goal is walkable -- $1 goals
chain.why: A goal has a position in data/chain.json and no number in a file name, so there is no numbering to report.

chain.pattern: ^(chain: every goal is walkable -- \d+ goals), (?:the run stands on `[a-z0-9-]+`, \d+ of \d+|no goal is installed)
chain.why: nv names the installed goal and its position as `N of M`, which chain.py read as a bare number from .loop/chain.json.

plan.why: A message names the program that printed it.
`--past` names the program it counts the registers with.
`nv owners --check` refuses a gap tagged to a past milestone on its own, and takes the flag only so a carried floor check still passes it.
A goal tagged with a label such as `dossier` or `post-parity` has a null milestone in its record, so nv lists the goals in no milestone and has no label to name.
A milestone file and a status field are printed as written, so a command they name is the same text on both sides, and the rewrite every group applies to the Python side is applied to nv's too.
